props.title: Killer of Sheep
props.initialSlug: A boy's harsh life in Watts defies easy escape

sections.content: Killer of Sheep (1978) stands as Charles Burnett's raw, poetic masterpiece of African American neorealism. Shot on 16mm for under $10,000 while Burnett was a UCLA film student, it captures daily life in LA's Watts neighborhood with documentary-like intimacy. The film follows Stan, a slaughterhouse worker whose soul-crushing job and economic hardship affect his family relationships. Like Italian neorealist classics Bicycle Thieves (1948) and Rome, Open City (1945), Burnett uses non-professional actors and real locations to achieve stunning authenticity.

sections.content: Burnett's film pioneered what would become known as the L.A. Rebellion film movement, where Black filmmakers challenged Hollywood conventions with personal, politically conscious cinema. The movement included vital works like Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song (1971) and To Sleep with Anger (1990). These filmmakers rejected both mainstream stereotypes and blaxploitation tropes, instead crafting nuanced portraits of Black life with European art film influences.

The film's stunning black and white photography transforms Watts into a landscape of profound visual poetry. Children playing in dusty lots and jumping between rooftops become balletic sequences set to blues and jazz. Like The Last Black Man in San Francisco (2019), it finds beauty in urban spaces while addressing displacement and gentrification. The slaughterhouse scenes, reminiscent of Georges Franju's Blood of the Beasts (1949), create powerful metaphors for economic violence. SUBHEAD: Impact and Legacy

sections.content: Burnett's naturalistic approach influenced a generation of independent filmmakers, from Barry Jenkins' Moonlight (2016) to Gus Van Sant's Mala Noche (1986). The film's poetry-of-the-everyday aesthetic can be traced through American indie landmarks like George Washington (2000) and The Florida Project (2017). Its unflinching look at labor and class struggles echoes in contemporary works like Sorry to Bother You (2018).
